query: We are investigating a specific eutectic high entropy alloy (comprising Al, Co, Cr, Fe, Ni) that exhibits a dual-phase lamellar structure and suffers from catastrophic interfacial cracking and low ductility. The operating regime is room temperature uniaxial tension. Known failures include the strength-ductility trade-off and stress concentration at phase interfaces. Design constraints require maintaining the alloy composition while altering the microstructure to arrest interfacial cracking and promote uniform plasticity. Propose a high-intensity thermomechanical treatment hypothesis that could transform the lamellar structure into a patterned configuration, explain the predicted boundary conditions for success (e.g., specific temperature/pressure windows), and define a falsification experiment involving conventional hot isostatic pressing to isolate the effect of extreme pressure.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a high-intensity thermomechanical treatment (HITMT) involving severe plastic deformation (SPD) at elevated temperatures (0.6–0.7 Tm) followed by controlled cooling can transform the continuous lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 EHEA into a patterned, discontinuous, or equiaxed grain configuration. This transformation is predicted to interrupt continuous phase interfaces, thereby arresting interfacial cracking and promoting uniform plasticity via enhanced strain hardening and dislocation storage, ultimately breaking the strength-ductility trade-off.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a fine, continuous lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, exhibiting high strength but limited ductility due to catastrophic interfacial cracking under room temperature uniaxial tension.
generation.intervention: High-intensity thermomechanical treatment (HITMT): Severe plastic deformation (e.g., High Pressure Torsion or Equal Channel Angular Pressing) performed at elevated temperatures (600–800°C, approx. 0.6–0.7 Tm) to induce dynamic recrystallization and break up the lamellar structure, followed by a controlled cooling rate to stabilize a patterned or equiaxed grain structure.
generation.conditions: Temperature: 600–800°C (0.6–0.7 Tm); Pressure: >1 GPa (for SPD); Strain rate: High (10^-1 to 10^0 s^-1); Atmosphere: Inert (Ar) to prevent oxidation; Post-treatment: Controlled cooling.
generation.structural_mediator: Disruption of continuous lamellar interfaces and formation of a patterned or equiaxed grain structure with high-angle grain boundaries, which act as barriers to crack propagation and promote uniform dislocation slip.
generation.mechanism: The high-intensity thermomechanical treatment induces dynamic recrystallization and grain refinement, breaking the continuous lamellar fcc/B2 interfaces. This reduces stress concentration sites at phase boundaries and promotes uniform plasticity by enabling more homogeneous dislocation distribution and strain hardening, thereby mitigating interfacial cracking.
generation.predicted_outcome: Significant improvement in room temperature ductility (elongation >20%) and maintained or enhanced strength, with a reduction in catastrophic interfacial cracking and a more uniform deformation behavior under uniaxial tension.
generation.baseline: As-cast AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 EHEA with lamellar fcc/B2 structure, showing high strength but low ductility due to interfacial cracking.
generation.boundary: The treatment must be applied within the temperature window of 600–800°C to ensure dynamic recrystallization without excessive grain growth or phase decomposition. Pressure must be sufficient to induce severe plastic deformation (>1 GPa).
generation.uncertainty: The exact temperature and pressure windows for optimal microstructure transformation are not precisely defined in the available literature. There is a risk of excessive grain growth or phase instability if the treatment parameters are not carefully controlled. The long-term stability of the patterned structure under cyclic loading is also uncertain.
generation.falsification_experiment: Perform conventional Hot Isostatic Pressing (HIP) on the as-cast AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 EHEA at 1400°C and 200 MPa for 2 hours (conditions similar to those in PMC6926650). If the lamellar structure remains largely intact and ductility does not significantly improve compared to the HITMT-treated samples, it would falsify the hypothesis that high-intensity thermomechanical treatment is necessary to transform the microstructure and improve ductility. The HIP treatment should not induce the same level of severe plastic deformation and dynamic recrystallization as the HITMT, thus serving as a control to isolate the effect of extreme pressure and deformation.

cited_evidence.text:
High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

As such, our alloy design strategy resulted in the discovery of an EHEA with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 structure and balanced high fracture strength and high ductility. This novel strategy is promising to solve the problems inhibiting the engineering application of HEAs as high-temperature materials, including the inferior castability and compositional segregation, and the conflict between high fracture strength and high ductility. In addition, this novel strategy also brought breakthrough to NiAl-based alloys in significantly enhancing the ductility at room temperature while simultaneously achieving the high strength. The EHEA concept, combining the advantages of both HEAs and eutectic alloys, and at the same time eliminating the disadvantages of these two types of alloys, leads to a promising new class of high-temperature alloys. Using this new alloy design strategy, an industrial scale HEA with uniform organizations and compositions can be prepared by the conventional casting method in a low cost way, allowing for large-scale industrial applications.
